subtitle: How SPKI certificates prove authorization, not identity.

tldr.problem: Digital certificates were traditionally used to bind names to keys (identity), but applications actually need to know whether a key holder is authorized to do something, not what their name is.
tldr.mechanism: SPKI certificates directly bind authorizations to keys (or names, which then resolve to keys), allowing applications to check permissions without first resolving a name. The SPKI framework also enables local names (meaningful to individuals) to scale globally through SDSI name chaining, and supports delegation of permissions through a certificate chain.
tldr.outcome: SPKI presents a theoretical framework for authorization-based certificates with delegation, validity conditions, and name management. It remains an experimental protocol influential in security research but not widely deployed in practice.

today: RFC 2693 is Experimental. SPKI remains an influential theoretical framework for authorization-based security, with ideas reflected in modern zero-trust and decentralized identity systems. However, it has not seen widespread deployment as a standardized protocol; most systems continue to use identity-based certificates with access control lists.

sections.title: Authorization vs. Identity
sections.content:
Certificates have traditionally bound names to keys: they say a key belongs to someone named Alice. But when a system decides whether to grant access, it does not care what Alice's name is. It cares whether Alice is authorized. RFC 2693 presents a different model: certificates that bind authorizations directly to keys.

This shift has several consequences. Applications no longer need to resolve a person's name; they can check permissions directly. A single issuer is trusted for authorization, rather than needing separate issuers for identity and authorization. And permissions can be delegated through a chain of certificates, allowing access decisions to be distributed across an organization without a central access control list.
sections.eli5: Instead of asking is this person named Alice, you ask is this person authorized. That is simpler and makes it easier to share power.

sections.title: Local and Global Names
sections.content:
Practical systems use names. SPKI embraces this by adopting SDSI (Simple Distributed Security Infrastructure) names, which are local to their definer. Alice can define a name fred in her namespace; Bob can use alice:fred to refer to the same entity in Bob's own lookups. Names can chain: alice:(name fred sam) refers to an entity that Alice calls fred and fred calls sam. This allows local names to be meaningful and short while still being usable globally without requiring a single global naming authority. When a global identifier is needed, the public key or its hash serves this purpose.

A fully qualified SDSI name combines a public key (identifying the namespace) with one or more local names within that namespace. For example: (name (hash sha1 |TLCgPLFlGTzgUbcaYLW8kGTEnUk=|) jim therese) is a fully qualified name using an SHA-1 hash of a public key as the identifier of the namespace and a two-name chain to specify the entity.
sections.eli5: You have a personal address book where you call someone Jim. Your friend has an address book where the same person is Therese's assistant. You can refer to both names together to identify who you mean.

sections.title: Certificates and ACLs
sections.content: SPKI defines three methods of granting authorization. Attribute certificates (from X.509v3) bind an authorization to a name, requiring a separate identity certificate to map the name to a key. X.509v3 extensions allow a single certificate to carry both a name and authorization. SPKI authorization certificates directly bind authorization to a key, separating the low-security mapping from key to name (for investigation) from the high-security authorization. ACL entries (Access Control Lists) function like unsigned certificate bodies: they grant permissions locally, anchoring certificate chains. An ACL for a resource is the source of empowerment; certificates then propagate that empowerment downstream. An ACL entry can have a key, a name, or a threshold function (k of n keys must agree) as its subject.
sections.eli5: An access list on a door says who can enter. A certificate from the boss saying someone can enter adds to that. If the boss delegates to managers, each manager can issue their own certificates.

sections.title: Delegating Permission
sections.content: A key power of SPKI is delegation: a certificate can grant permission and allow the holder to delegate it further, or grant permission without delegation rights. SPKI chose boolean delegation control: a delegation flag is either true (delegable) or false (not delegable). This avoids the problem of predicting depth (how many levels of delegation to allow) while preventing a delegator who cannot delegate from setting up proxy services to circumvent the restriction. When delegation is permitted, the holder can delegate the same permission or a subset of it to others. This enables organizations to distribute access control without relying on a central authority: each manager can decide who under them has access, without asking the top authority each time.
sections.eli5: A manager with permission to hire can say to a team lead, you can also decide who to hire. The team lead can then pick individual hirers without asking the manager each time.

sections.title: Certificate Validation and Validity Conditions
sections.content:
Processing a set of certificates to reach an authorization decision involves three stages. First, individual certificates are verified by checking signatures and any on-line tests (such as Certificate Revocation Lists or re-validations). They are mapped to intermediate forms called tuples (five-element intermediate structures representing the issuer, subject, delegation flag, authorization, and validity dates). Second, uses of local names are replaced with the keys they resolve to. Third, authorization tuples are reduced to a final authorization result. Two 5-tuples can be combined if their issuer/subject chain matches and delegation is allowed, intersecting the authorizations and validity dates in the process.

Validity conditions can be simple date ranges, or they can involve on-line checks. SPKI permits timed CRLs (revocation lists with validity dates that must not overlap), timed revalidations (positive confirmations with dates), or one-time revalidations (on-line checks with a nonce, valid for only one authorization computation).
sections.eli5: Checking a permission is like following a chain of notes. You start with the resource owner's permission. Then you follow each delegated permission, checking dates and signatures. You end with yes or no.

sections.title: Trust and Key Management
sections.content: The security of SPKI depends on the integrity of root keys (in ACLs) and the proper revocation of compromised keys. Key management strategies include publishing keys directly (inescapable identifiers for individuals, though politically challenging), publishing through a naming authority, or using (name, key) certificates. Short-lived keys reduce the impact of compromise. Threshold ACL subjects (k of n keys must agree) provide fault tolerance. The SPKI framework addresses security by ensuring deterministic authorization computations: the result does not depend on timing of CRL delivery or other non-deterministic factors. A compromised issuer or revoked certificate can be detected through properly timed CRLs or revalidations, and the impact can be limited by restricting delegation and using short validity intervals.
sections.eli5: Keep important keys safe. If a key leaks, revoke certificates signed by it quickly. Use multiple keys for big decisions so one leak does not break everything.
